description:
Crypto-security supplement complementary to JMAP-sf5h.9 (which asks the workspace to defend `#[serde(try_from = "String")]` over a custom `Deserialize` impl). This finding adds the protocol-boundary security angle that .9 doesn't cover.

**Current shape** (digest.rs:99-102):

```rust
#[serde(try_from = "String", into = "String")]
pub struct Sha256(String);
```

When deserializing a `Sha256` from JSON, serde_json takes the following path:

1. Parses the JSON string token and **allocates a Rust `String` of the full payload length**.
2. Calls `<Sha256 as TryFrom<String>>::try_from(s)`.
3. `from_hex` runs, observes `bytes.len() != 64`, returns `WrongLength`.
4. The allocated `String` is dropped.

**The problem**: step 1 happens **before** step 3. A hostile JMAP server (or upstream proxy, or any party able to inject into the response body — e.g. a malicious server, a tampered cache) sending `{"sha256": "aaa…a"}` with a 1 GiB string payload will cause the client to allocate 1 GiB before the type's own validator rejects the value. The 64-byte upper bound declared by the ABNF is **not enforced at allocation time** — it is enforced at validation time, after the buffer is materialized.

**Threat model** — this matters when:

- A JMAP client connects to an untrusted or compromised JMAP server. The server controls the response body and can pad any digest field arbitrarily.
- A JMAP client connects to a trusted JMAP server through an untrusted transport (e.g. a proxy that rewrites response bodies). Less likely on TLS, possible on metadata or via injection.
- A JMAP middleware (federation, mirror, cache) processes responses from a peer it does not fully trust. The chat-federation use case described in the workspace AGENTS.md is exactly this.

**Section C (untrusted input at protocol boundaries) requirement** that this fails:

> Variable-length fields have explicit upper bounds enforced before allocation. (Memory-DoS via "this field claims to be 4 GiB long".)

**Fix** — choose one, in order of decreasing cost-benefit:

(a) **Custom `Deserialize` via `Visitor::visit_str` with length pre-check**. Replace `#[serde(try_from = "String")]` with a hand-rolled `Deserialize` impl that uses a `Visitor` with `visit_str(&self, v: &str)` and rejects `v.len() != 64` before doing any allocation of its own. `serde_json`'s string deserializer still materializes the input into a `Cow<'de, str>` internally, but the borrowed-string path avoids the owned allocation when the input doesn't contain escape sequences. For digest payloads (which are pure ASCII), this means **zero `String` allocation on the rejection path**. This change is internal — public surface is unchanged. Bonus: closes JMAP-sf5h.22 (the clone-after-owning finding) for free, since the validating path operates on a borrow.

(b) **Document that allocation bounding lives in the consumer's transport layer**. Add a `# Allocation bounds` rustdoc section to `Sha256` stating: "This type does not bound allocation before validation. Consumers parsing `Sha256` from untrusted JMAP responses MUST enforce a body-size limit at the transport layer (e.g. `reqwest`'s response size limit, or a wrapping `Reader` with a hard byte cap). A hostile server can otherwise force `O(payload-length)` allocation per deserialize attempt before the 64-byte ABNF cap rejects the value." This is the minimum-cost option but offloads the bound onto every downstream consumer.

(c) **Both**. Implement (a) as defense-in-depth and add a shorter version of the (b) note explaining that the type now self-bounds at deserialize. Best option once .9 is resolved in favor of a custom `Deserialize` impl.

**Recommend (c)** as the resolution that subsumes (a) JMAP-sf5h.9 (idiom: defend the try_from routing) and (b) JMAP-sf5h.22 (clone-after-owning). The three findings are a single refactor.

What goes wrong if left as-is: a JMAP client deserializing responses from an untrusted server is one malicious response away from an O(server-controlled) allocation. Easy DoS for a remote attacker on a federation peer link.

title: Sha256 Deserialize path does not bound allocation before validation — memory-DoS posture at protocol boundary
